claim: DvPdf-GAL4 driver expresses strongly and specifically in the M cells and subsets of the E cells
source: To address further the roles of M and E cells, we made use of a recently described DvPdf-GAL4 driver, which expresses strongly and specifically in the M cells and subsets of the E cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bahn et al., 2009 and confirmed by experimental data showing GFP expression pattern

claim: GFP is expressed in the PDF-positive LNv cells and in several E cells in each hemisphere when DvPdf-GAL4 is crossed with UAS-mCD8::GFP
source: Exactly as reported (Bahn et al., 2009), GFP is expressed in the PDF-positive LNv cells and in several E cells in each hemisphere (Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by citation and experimental imaging data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The E cells labeled by DvPdf-GAL4 consist of the single PDF-negative 5th-sLNv and 4 LNds
source: the latter consist of the single PDF-negative 5th-sLNv (Figure 1C) and 4 LNds (subsequently referred to as the 5 Dv-E cells)
evidence: Supported by experimental imaging data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Rescuing PER expression with the DvPdf-GAL4 driver restored both morning and evening anticipation to the arrhythmic per01 strain
source: Rescuing PER expression with the DvPdf-GAL4 driver restored both morning and evening anticipation to the arrhythmic per01 strain (Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The five E cells labeled with DvPdf-GAL4, Pdf-gal80 project to the dorsal brain and to the accessory medulla
source: The five E cells labeled with DvPdf-GAL4, Pdf-gal80 (henceforth called the Dv-E driver and the Dv-E cells) project to the dorsal brain and to the accessory medulla (aMe) as previously described (Figure 1C, arrows) (Bahn et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation and experimental imaging data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Expression of DBTS in M cells does not change the locomotor activity pattern or phase
source: Although M cells (PDF neurons) are considered master pacemakers, neither expression of DBTS in M cells nor in its direct downstream target neurons-DN1ps (Zhang et al., 2010a, 2010b; Seluzicki et al., 2014) changes the locomotor activity pattern or phase (Figure 1D)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 1D and citations

claim: The evening peak phase is dramatically advanced when accelerating the endogenous clock in the 5 Dv-E cells
source: In contrast, the evening peak phase is dramatic advanced when accelerating the endogenous clock in the 5 Dv-E cells (Figure 1D)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 1D

claim: The E cells independently determine the major activity phase in LD
source: In contrast, the evening peak phase is dramatic advanced when accelerating the endogenous clock in the 5 Dv-E cells (Figure 1D), indicating that the E cells independently determine the major activity phase in LD (Stoleru et al., 2007)
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and supported by citation

claim: Differential neuron expression profiling suggests that the 5 Dv-E cells use excitatory neurotransmitter machinery to communicate with other neurons
source: Because differential neuron expression profiling suggests that the 5 Dv-E cells use excitatory neurotransmitter machinery to communicate with other neurons (unpublished data) (Johard et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by unpublished data and citation

claim: Dv-E GAL4/UAS-TNT flies have a severe circadian locomotor activity deficiency including significant attenuation of morning and evening anticipation
source: Compared to control flies, that is, flies that express inactive tetanus toxin UAS-Tet, Dv-E GAL4/UAS-TNT flies have a severe circadian locomotor activity deficiency. It includes a significant attenuation of morning anticipation as well as evening anticipation (Figure 2A, arrows)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Dv-E GAL4/UAS-TNT flies show a reduced major activity peak in DD and high levels of arrhythmicity
source: Compared to control flies, that is, flies that express inactive tetanus toxin UAS-Tet, Dv-E GAL4/UAS-TNT flies have a severe circadian locomotor activity deficiency. It includes a significant attenuation of morning anticipation as well as evening anticipation (Figure 2A, arrows), a reduced major activity peak in DD and high levels of arrhythmicity (Figure 2A; Table 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 2A and Table 1

claim: The mean locomotor activity of Dv-E GAL4/UAS-TNT flies compared to control flies was 44% in LD and 45% in DD
source: The mean locomotor activity of Dv-E GAL4/UAS-TNT flies compared to control flies was 44% in LD and 45% in DD.
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data

claim: Expression of the potassium channel Kir in the 5 Dv-E cells causes a significant reduction in both morning and evening anticipation as well as high percentage of DD arrhythmicity
source: Use of a different reagent, expression of the potassium channel Kir, to suppress neuronal activity in the 5 Dv-E cells also causes a significant reduction in both morning and evening anticipation as well as high percentage of DD arrhythmicity (Figure 2B, right, arrows and Table 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 2B and Table 1

claim: M cells impact wild-type E cell molecular oscillations
source: The M cells (s-LNvs) impact wild-type E cell molecular oscillations (Stoleru et al., 2005) as well as control DD rhythmicity
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: M cells control DD rhythmicity
source: The M cells (s-LNvs) impact wild-type E cell molecular oscillations (Stoleru et al., 2005) as well as control DD rhythmicity
evidence: Supported by established knowledge in the field

claim: Temporal expression of PERS in M cells shortened the circadian period to 20.5 hr
source: This protocol should temporally express PERS, which indeed shortened the circadian period to 20.5 hr (Figure 3A; Table 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 3A and Table 1

claim: Short-term drug feeding is sufficient to induce the transgene and accelerate circadian period to generate an approximate 14 hr phase advance at the end of the protocol
source: Since sibling flies on normal food maintained a normal 23.5 hr period and returning the flies to normal food also reversed the short period to 23.5 hr, short-term drug feeding is sufficient to induce the transgene and accelerate circadian period to generate an approximate 14 hr phase advance at the end of the protocol (Figure 3A,B)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 3A and 3B

claim: Flies co-expressing PDF RNAi along with UAS-perS showed no short period phenotype
source: Flies co-expressing PDF RNAi along with UAS-perS showed no short period phenotype (Figure 3A,B)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 3A and 3B

claim: PDF cells may not express a classical neurotransmitter that causes E cells to follow accelerated PDF neurons
source: A series of control RNAi and tetanus toxin light chain (TNT) constructs suggests that the effect is specific to this single neuropeptide. For example, PDF cells may not express a classical neurotransmitter that causes E cells to follow accelerated PDF neurons (Figure 3C)
evidence: Inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Temporal co-expression of the inwardly rectifying potassium channel (Kir) with UAS-perS inhibited the short period phenotype
source: Temporal co-expression of the inwardly rectifying potassium channel (Kir) with UAS-perS similarly inhibited the short period phenotype, indicating that PDF cell firing is also required for maintaining PDF-mediated communication from M cells (Figure 3A,B)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 3A and 3B

claim: PDF cell firing is required for maintaining PDF-mediated communication from M cells
source: Temporal co-expression of the inwardly rectifying potassium channel (Kir) with UAS-perS similarly inhibited the short period phenotype, indicating that PDF cell firing is also required for maintaining PDF-mediated communication from M cells (Figure 3A,B)
evidence: Inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 3A and 3B

claim: Circadian period is determined by multiple independent oscillators, M cells and subset of E cells, which are coordinated by PDF signaling
source: A recent paper also concluded that circadian period is determined by multiple independent oscillators, M cells and subset of E cells, which are coordinated by PDF signaling (Yao and Shafer, 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: PDF-cell firing and PDF generate the M cell resetting signal
source: The data taken together indicate that PDF-cell firing and PDF generate the M cell resetting signal.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results

claim: A 2 hr temperature shift of DvPdf-GAL4/UAS-dTrpA1 flies from 21°C to 30°C at ZT15 caused a phase delay of approximately 3–4 hr
source: This protocol caused a phase delay of approximately 3–4 hr (Figure 4A), similar to the delay caused by a 2 hr saturating (2000 lux) light pulse at ZT15 (Bao et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 4A and citation

claim: Addition of Pdf-GAL80 to DvPdf-GAL4 dramatically reduced the phase-shift
source: Addition of Pdf-GAL80 to DvPdf-GAL4, that is, use of the Dv-E driver, had a dramatically reduced phase-shift, which indicates that PDF morning cell firing is necessary for the DvPdf-GAL4 firing-induced phase-shift
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data and inference

claim: PDF morning cell firing is necessary for the DvPdf-GAL4 firing-induced phase-shift
source: Addition of Pdf-GAL80 to DvPdf-GAL4, that is, use of the Dv-E driver, had a dramatically reduced phase-shift, which indicates that PDF morning cell firing is necessary for the DvPdf-GAL4 firing-induced phase-shift
evidence: Inferred from experimental data

claim: A 2-hr temperature shift of Pdf-GAL4/UAS-dTrpA1 flies at ZT15 elicited a similar 3-hr phase delay
source: Firing was next restricted to PDF neurons, that is, a 2-hr temperature shift of Pdf-GAL4/UAS-dTrpA1 flies at ZT15. This protocol elicited a similar 3-hr phase delay (Figure 4A)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 4A

claim: PDF morning cell firing is sufficient for a quasi-normal firing-mediated phase-shift at ZT15
source: This protocol elicited a similar 3-hr phase delay (Figure 4A), indicating that PDF morning cell firing is not only necessary but also sufficient for a quasi-normal firing-mediated phase-shift at ZT15
evidence: Inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Firing of morning pacemakers causes proper phase advances at ZT21
source: Firing of morning pacemakers also causes proper phase advances at ZT21, and control flies with TrpA1 expression in E cells but not in M cells show no phase advance (Figure 4B and data not shown)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Control flies with TrpA1 expression in E cells but not in M cells show no phase advance
source: Firing of morning pacemakers also causes proper phase advances at ZT21, and control flies with TrpA1 expression in E cells but not in M cells show no phase advance (Figure 4B and data not shown)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data

claim: PDF cell firing mimics light-induced phase-shifting
source: This indicates that PDF cell firing more broadly mimics light-induced phase-shifting
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing phase delays and advances

claim: Firing of dopaminergic neuronal group with TH-GAL4 had little or no phase-shifting effect
source: It is also notable that firing of many other neuronal subsets, including the strongly activity-promoting dopaminergic neuronal group with TH-GAL4, had little or no phase-shifting effect (Figure 4A and data not shown)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 4A

claim: A 2 hr 30°C pulse alone is unable to cause a substantial phase-shift
source: These negative results confirm that a 2 hr 30°C pulse alone is unable to cause a substantial phase-shift
evidence: Inferred from control experiments

claim: The perS mutation shortens circadian period to 19 hr
source: This is because previous studies had shown that the perS mutation not only shortens circadian period to 19 hr but also dramatically alters light-induced phase-shifting, from a low amplitude type 1 PRC to a high amplitude type 0 PRC (Bao et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: The perS mutation dramatically alters light-induced phase-shifting, from a low amplitude type 1 PRC to a high amplitude type 0 PRC
source: This is because previous studies had shown that the perS mutation not only shortens circadian period to 19 hr but also dramatically alters light-induced phase-shifting, from a low amplitude type 1 PRC to a high amplitude type 0 PRC (Bao et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Neuronal firing induced an exaggerated phase change in a perS background compared to wild type in the advance zone (maximum 6–7 hr)
source: Similar to light, neuronal firing induced an exaggerated phase change in a perS background compared to wild type in the advance zone (maximum 6–7 hr; Figure 4C)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 4C

claim: The phase-shifts of parental control strains without dTrpA1 expression were statistically indistinguishable from unheated groups
source: The phase-shifts of parental control strains without dTrpA1 expression were statistically indistinguishable from unheated groups, further indicating that the 2 hr 30°C pulse has no phase-shifting effect (Kaushik et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data and citation

claim: Addition of Pdf-GAL80 to the perS; DvPdf-GAL4; UAS-dTrpA1 background dramatically reduced both advance and delay phase-shifts
source: Addition of Pdf-GAL80 to the perS; DvPdf-GAL4; UAS-dTrpA1 background dramatically reduced both advance and delay phase-shifts (data not shown)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data

claim: Morning cell activity makes the major contribution to the generation of enhanced phase-shift in perS background
source: Addition of Pdf-GAL80 to the perS; DvPdf-GAL4; UAS-dTrpA1 background dramatically reduced both advance and delay phase-shifts (data not shown), confirming that morning cell activity makes the major contribution to the generation of this enhanced phase-shift
evidence: Inferred from experimental data

claim: PDF contributes to phase-shifting in other insects
source: We note that the ability of PDF to contribute to phase-shifting has been previously demonstrated in other insects (Petri and Stengl, 1997)
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: A mutant in PDFR (pdfr5304 flies) exhibits a reduced morning peak and a phase advanced evening peak in LD
source: Like pdf01 mutant flies, a mutant in PDFR (pdfr5304 flies) exhibits a reduced morning peak and a phase advanced evening peak in LD as well as a short period and a high percentage of arrhythmic flies in DD (Hyun et al., 2005; Lear et al., 2005) (Figure 5A, left)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 5A and citations

claim: A mutant in PDFR (pdfr5304 flies) exhibits a short period and a high percentage of arrhythmic flies in DD
source: Like pdf01 mutant flies, a mutant in PDFR (pdfr5304 flies) exhibits a reduced morning peak and a phase advanced evening peak in LD as well as a short period and a high percentage of arrhythmic flies in DD (Hyun et al., 2005; Lear et al., 2005) (Figure 5A, left)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 5A and citations

claim: A large number of circadian cells including M and E cells normally express PDFR
source: Although a large number of circadian cells including M and E cells normally express PDFR (Im et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Restricting PDFR expression to only the 5 Dv-E cells of pdfr5304 flies rescued essentially all major circadian deficiencies
source: we could restrict PDFR expression to only the 5 Dv-E cells of pdfr5304 flies with the DvPdf-GAL4, Pdf-GAL80 driver expressing PDFR in the pdfr5304 background. Essentially all major circadian deficiencies were rescued (Figure 5A, middle compared to 5A left and Table 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 5A and Table 1

claim: CRY and PDFR are co-expressed in the same groups of circadian cells
source: Because CRY and PDFR are co-expressed in the same groups of circadian cells (Im et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Inhibiting PDFR expression in CRY-positive Dv-E cells with Cry-GAL80 almost completely eliminated the rescue of the morning, evening peaks and rhythmicity on the pdfr5304; DvPdf-GAL4, Pdf-GAL80/UAS-PDFR flies
source: we inhibited PDFR expression in CRY-positive Dv-E cells with Cry-GAL80. This almost completely eliminated the rescue of the morning, evening peaks and rhythmicity on the pdfr5304; DvPdf-GAL4, Pdf-GAL80/UAS-PDFR flies (Figure 5A, right compared to Figure 5A, middle and Table 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 5A and Table 1

claim: The CRY-positive subset of Dv-E cells are the key targets of PDF and make the major contribution to circadian behavior in LD as well as DD
source: This almost completely eliminated the rescue of the morning, evening peaks and rhythmicity on the pdfr5304; DvPdf-GAL4, Pdf-GAL80/UAS-PDFR flies (Figure 5A, right compared to Figure 5A, middle and Table 1), suggesting that it is the CRY-positive subset of Dv-E cells that are the key targets of PDF and that makes the major contribution to circadian behavior in LD as well as DD
evidence: Inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 5A and Table 1

claim: There is a single CRY-positive LNd among the Dv-E cells
source: To localize these CRY-positive Dv-E cells, we stained DvPdf-GAL4, Pdf-GAL80>UAS-mCD8:GFP brains with an anti-CRY antibody and identified a single LNd (Figure 5B, arrow) as well as the 5th small LNv ([Yoshii et al., 2008] and data not shown)
evidence: Supported by experimental imaging data shown in Figure 5B and citation

claim: The 5th small LNv is CRY-positive
source: To localize these CRY-positive Dv-E cells, we stained DvPdf-GAL4, Pdf-GAL80>UAS-mCD8:GFP brains with an anti-CRY antibody and identified a single LNd (Figure 5B, arrow) as well as the 5th small LNv ([Yoshii et al., 2008] and data not shown)
evidence: Supported by experimental imaging data and citation

claim: Adding a copy of Cry-GAL80 to DvPdf-GAL4>UAS-mCD8:GFP flies eliminated GFP expression in the single CRY-positive LNd and the 5th-sLNv but not in M cells
source: To confirmed that there is only 1 CRY-positive LNd, adding a copy of Cry-GAL80 to DvPdf-GAL4>UAS-mCD8:GFP flies eliminated GFP expression in that single LNd and the 5th-sLNv (Figure 5C; arrow points to a fiber from CRY+ LNd to the accessory medulla [Yoshii et al., 2008]) but not in M cells (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by experimental imaging data shown in Figure 5C and citation

claim: The 2 CRY+ Dv-E cells play a more important circadian and activity role
source: Based on the behavior (Figure 5A), these 2 CRY+ Dv-E cells play a more important circadian and activity role
evidence: Inferred from behavioral data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The magnitude of the phase-shift was severely inhibited in pdfr5304 flies
source: The magnitude of the phase-shift was severely inhibited in pdfr5304 flies, consistent with the importance of PDF signaling for communication (Figure 5D)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Expressing PDFR and dTrpA1 with the DvPdf driver rescued both phase delays and advances in pdfr5304 flies
source: The magnitude of the phase-shift was severely inhibited in pdfr5304 flies, consistent with the importance of PDF signaling for communication (Figure 5D), and expressing PDFR and dTrpA1 with the DvPdf driver rescued both phase delays and advances
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data

claim: Rescue of PDFR expression in PDF cell and CRY negative Dv-E cells with DvPdf-GAL4; Cry-GAL80 driver is not sufficient to rescue the major circadian deficiency
source: Also because rescue of PDFR expression in PDF cell and CRY negative Dv-E cells with DvPdf-GAL4; Cry-GAL80 driver is not sufficient to rescue the major circadian deficiency (Figure 5A; Table 1; Lear et al., 2009) and phase-shifting of the PDFR mutant strain (Figure 5D)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 5A, Table 1, Figure 5D and citation

claim: PDFR expression in the 5 Dv-E cells, especially in the 2 CRY+ Dv-E cells, is sufficient to rescue PDF cell firing-induced phase-shifting
source: we favor the interpretation that PDFR expression in the 5 Dv-E cells, especially in the 2 CRY+ Dv-E cells, is sufficient to rescue PDF cell firing-induced phase-shifting like its rescue of circadian behavior (Figure 5C)
evidence: Inferred from experimental data

claim: Firing of morning cells releases PDF and a subsequent association with its cognate receptor on Dv-E cells is important for both phase delays and advances
source: The data taken together suggest that firing of morning cells releases PDF and that a subsequent association with its cognate receptor on Dv-E cells is important for both phase delays and advances
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results

claim: Rapid CRY-dependent TIM degradation is a key event in light or heat-mediated phase-shifting
source: Because rapid CRY-dependent TIM degradation is a key event in light or heat-mediated phase-shifting (Suri et al., 1998; Yang et al., 1998)
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: M cell firing causes a dramatic and rapid reduction of TIM but not PER staining intensity in circadian neurons after firing at ZT15
source: There was indeed a dramatic and rapid reduction of TIM but not PER staining intensity in circadian neurons after M cell firing at ZT15 when TIM and PER are cytoplasmic (Figure 6A,B)
evidence: Supported by experimental imaging data shown in Figure 6A and 6B

claim: The staining intensity of control flies without dTrpA1 expression was unaffected by the temperature shift
source: the staining intensity of control flies without dTrpA1 expression was unaffected by the temperature shift (Figure 6D)
evidence: Supported by experimental imaging data shown in Figure 6D

claim: M cell firing caused nuclear TIM degradation in all circadian neurons at ZT21
source: M cell firing also caused nuclear TIM degradation in all circadian neurons at ZT21 (Figure 6E)
evidence: Supported by experimental imaging data shown in Figure 6E

claim: TIM levels were dramatically reduced after ATP application in Pdf-GAL4; UAS-p2x2; cry01 brains
source: TIM levels were dramatically reduced after ATP application, and there was no significant effect in control cry01 flies (Figure 7A)
evidence: Supported by experimental imaging data shown in Figure 7A

claim: There was no significant effect on TIM levels in control cry01 flies after ATP application
source: TIM levels were dramatically reduced after ATP application, and there was no significant effect in control cry01 flies (Figure 7A)
evidence: Supported by experimental imaging data shown in Figure 7A

claim: In vitro P2X2 activation mimics the effects of in vivo dTrpA1 activation on TIM degradation
source: The results mimic the similar effects of in vivo dTrpA1 activation, confirming that PDF neuron firing causes TIM degradation
evidence: Inferred from comparison of experimental results

claim: PDF neuron firing causes TIM degradation
source: The results mimic the similar effects of in vivo dTrpA1 activation, confirming that PDF neuron firing causes TIM degradation
evidence: Inferred from experimental data

claim: The canonical cell-autonomous model for TIM degradation and phase-shifting requires functional CRY
source: The canonical cell-autonomous model for TIM degradation and phase-shifting requires functional CRY (Emery et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Firing-induced phase-shifting is CRY-independent
source: However, the in vitro P2X2 results suggest that firing-induced phase-shifting is CRY-independent
evidence: Inferred from experimental results

claim: Light pulses failed to change the phase of DvPdf-GAL4, UAS-dTrpA1; cry01 flies
source: Light pulses failed to change the phase of these DvPdf-GAL4, UAS-dTrpA1; cry01 flies as expected from the role of CRY in photoreception (data not shown)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data

claim: DvPdf-GAL4, UAS-dTrpA1; cry01 flies still responded to M cell firing
source: Light pulses failed to change the phase of these DvPdf-GAL4, UAS-dTrpA1; cry01 flies as expected from the role of CRY in photoreception (data not shown), but they still responded to M cell firing
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data

claim: ZT21 phase advances showed a dramatic 10-hr advance in the cry01 background
source: Although ZT21 phase advances showed a dramatic and enigmatic 10-hr advance in this background (Figure 7B)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 7B

claim: ZT15 phase delays in the cry01 background were only marginally different from wild-type
source: Although ZT21 phase advances showed a dramatic and enigmatic 10-hr advance in this background (Figure 7B), ZT15 phase delays in the cry01 background were only marginally different from wild-type
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data

claim: Phase delays may be more simply firing-dependent than advances
source: This suggests that delays may be more simply firing-dependent than advances, which may respond to a more complicated combination of light and firing
evidence: Inferred from experimental data

claim: Phase advances may respond to a more complicated combination of light and firing
source: This suggests that delays may be more simply firing-dependent than advances, which may respond to a more complicated combination of light and firing
evidence: Speculative inference from experimental data

claim: The pacemaker firing paradigm dramatically reduced TIM levels in circadian neurons at ZT21 in cry01 brains, especially in the LNds
source: Like the results in a wild-type strain, the pacemaker firing paradigm dramatically reduced TIM levels in these circadian neurons at ZT21, especially in the LNds; this further confirms that the neuronal firing-phase resetting pathway does not require CRY (Figure 7C)
evidence: Supported by experimental imaging data shown in Figure 7C

claim: The neuronal firing-phase resetting pathway does not require CRY
source: Like the results in a wild-type strain, the pacemaker firing paradigm dramatically reduced TIM levels in these circadian neurons at ZT21, especially in the LNds; this further confirms that the neuronal firing-phase resetting pathway does not require CRY (Figure 7C)
evidence: Inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Neural firing causes TIM degradation and phase resetting, which are controlled by a mechanism at least partially independent of CRY-mediated protein degradation
source: Our data taken together indicate that neural firing causes TIM degradation and phase resetting, which are controlled by a mechanism at least partially independent of CRY-mediated protein degradation
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results

claim: The E3 ubiquitin ligase component Cullin-3 (CUL-3) regulates TIM degradation and promotes TIM/PER oscillations in DD
source: The E3 ubiquitin ligase component Cullin-3 (CUL-3) was recently shown to regulate TIM degradation and promote TIM/PER oscillations in DD (Grima et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: The effect of CUL-3 is particularly striking when TIM is cytoplasmic in the early night
source: Moreover, the effect of CUL-3 is particularly striking when TIM is cytoplasmic in the early night
evidence: Supported by citation to Grima et al., 2012

claim: Co-expression of CUL-3 RNAi with dTrpA1 under DvPdf-GAL4 control did not significantly affect DD rhythmicity and period at 21°C
source: Indeed, co-expression of CUL-3 RNAi with dTrpA1 under DvPdf-GAL4 control did not significantly affect DD rhythmicity and period at 21°C (Table 1; Grima et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Table 1 and citation

claim: Co-expression of CUL-3 RNAi with dTrpA1 under DvPdf-GAL4 control reduced firing-mediated phase delays at ZT15
source: However, these flies had reduced firing-mediated phase delays at ZT15 (Figure 8A)
evidence: Supported by experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 8A

claim: Co-expression of CUL-3 RNAi with dTrpA1 substantially reduced TIM degradation in DvPdf-GAL4 labeled M and E cells
source: TIM staining revealed that the co-expression also substantially reduced TIM degradation in DvPdf-GAL4 labeled M and E cells (Figure 8B,C)
evidence: Supported by experimental imaging data shown in Figure 8B and 8C

claim: TIM degradation within the DNs was potent and indistinguishable from control strains when CUL-3 RNAi was co-expressed
source: In contrast, TIM degradation within the DNs was potent and indistinguishable from control strains, presumably because the DvPdf-GAL4 driver and UAS constructs are not expressed in the DNs (Figure 8B)
evidence: Supported by experimental imaging data shown in Figure 8B

claim: The effects of the CUL-3 RNAi constructs are principally cell-autonomous
source: This suggests that the effects of the CUL-3 RNAi constructs are principally cell-autonomous and that dTrpA1-mediated M cell-firing remains potent despite co-expression of the RNAi constructs
evidence: Inferred from experimental data

claim: dTrpA1-mediated M cell-firing remains potent despite co-expression of the CUL-3 RNAi constructs
source: This suggests that the effects of the CUL-3 RNAi constructs are principally cell-autonomous and that dTrpA1-mediated M cell-firing remains potent despite co-expression of the RNAi constructs
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing TIM degradation in DNs

claim: M cell firing in the early night activates a PDFR-CUL-3 pathway to reduce cytoplasmic TIM accumulation
source: The results taken together indicate that M cell firing in the early night activates a PDFR-CUL-3 pathway to reduce cytoplasmic TIM accumulation
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results

claim: TIM levels within the DvPdf-GAL4-labeled pacemakers make a substantial contribution to the magnitude of the phase delay
source: The results also imply that TIM levels within the DvPdf-GAL4-labeled pacemakers make a substantial contribution to the magnitude of the phase delay
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing correlation between TIM degradation and phase delay magnitude

claim: E cells are major pacemakers under more natural L-D conditions
source: We therefore suggest that E cells are major pacemakers under more natural L-D conditions and that M cells serve principally to integrate light information and phase adjust the E cells through firing and PDF release (Figure 9)
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results

claim: M cells serve principally to integrate light information and phase adjust the E cells through firing and PDF release
source: We therefore suggest that E cells are major pacemakers under more natural L-D conditions and that M cells serve principally to integrate light information and phase adjust the E cells through firing and PDF release (Figure 9)
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results

claim: The 5 Dv-E cells are responsible for the evening anticipation peak and its timing
source: First, the 5 Dv-E cells are not only responsible for the evening anticipation peak and its timing, but they also contribute to the morning peak, free running rhythms and total activity
evidence: Inferred from experimental results

claim: The 5 Dv-E cells contribute to the morning peak, free running rhythms and total activity
source: First, the 5 Dv-E cells are not only responsible for the evening anticipation peak and its timing, but they also contribute to the morning peak, free running rhythms and total activity
evidence: Inferred from experimental results

claim: The 5 Dv-E cells play a key role in all aspects of circadian rhythms and locomotor activity
source: Otherwise put, these cells appear to play a key role in all aspects of circadian rhythms and locomotor activity
evidence: Inferred from experimental results

claim: E cell resetting can occur in a non cell-autonomous manner, through M cell neuron firing, PDF release and E cell PDFR activation
source: Second, E cell resetting can occur in a non cell-autonomous manner, through M cell neuron firing, PDF release and E cell PDFR activation
evidence: Inferred from experimental results

claim: TIM level changes within the 5 Dv-E cells in response to M cell firing likely make a major contribution to the resulting phase changes, at least in the early night when phase delays occur
